facts.t: A postcard once became a Supreme Court writ petition
facts.d: Epistolary jurisdiction let letters, telegrams and even scribbled notes be treated as petitions. Balwant Singh (2010) later confined the practice to specific categories — bonded labour, children, environment, tribe and caste matters, women, and police brutality.

facts.t: Upendra Baxi renamed the whole enterprise
facts.d: He argued that American PIL protects interests without groups, like consumer rights, while India's protects interests within groups — the marginalised. He preferred the term Social Action Litigation, and the distinction still frames the academic debate.

facts.t: PIL created the CBI's operational autonomy
facts.d: Vineet Narain (1997) arose from the hawala diaries and produced binding directions on the agency's independence. A citizen petition restructured a central investigative agency — with no legislation involved at any stage.

bank.q: Public interest litigation was first used by the Supreme Court in:
o: Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union v. UoI
bank.e: Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union. S. P. Gupta (1982) then liberalised locus standi decisively.

bank.q: With reference to the features of PIL, consider the following statements:
s: Locus standi is relaxed so that anyone may file for the rights of others.
Proceedings are non-adversarial and cooperative rather than combative.
Courts may appoint expert commissions for fact-finding.
bank.e: All three are correct — the third from Sheela Barse v. State of Maharashtra.

bank.q: Match List I (case) with List II (right expanded through PIL):
bank.e: Olga Tellis on livelihood, Unnikrishnan on education, PUCL on food, and M. C. Mehta on the environment.

bank.q: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised category for epistolary jurisdiction after Balwant Singh (2010)?
bank.e: Commercial disputes fall outside entirely. The permitted categories concern bonded labour, children, environment, tribe and caste issues, women and police brutality.

bank.as: Public interest litigation has been criticised for middle-class capture.
bank.rs: Its focus has shifted from the very poor towards civic and lifestyle concerns.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion — a criticism sharpened by Baxi's original framing of PIL as litigation for interests within marginalised groups.

bank.q: Consider the following criticisms of PIL:
s: Frivolous petitions filed for publicity or political motives.
Judicial overreach into the policy domain.
Reduction in the judiciary's ability to review administrative inaction.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are criticisms. PIL expanded review of administrative inaction — Vineet Narain is the leading example.

bank.q: Which case is cited for PIL being used as a tool for blackmail or settling personal scores?
o: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar
Ashok Kumar Pandey v. State of WB
bank.e: Ashok Kumar Pandey (2004). Subhash Kumar (1991) is cited for frivolous petitions, and SCBA for overreach into policy.

bank.q: All of the following are proposed ways forward for PIL EXCEPT:
o: Monitoring compliance through committees or amicus curiae
Developing community litigation through legal literacy
Using PILs to strengthen institutional remedies such as the NHRC and NGT
bank.e: Epistolary jurisdiction was restricted to defined categories in 2010, not abolished — and no proposal seeks its abolition.

bank.q: Who described PIL as a constitutional instrument to make justice accessible and governance accountable?
bank.e: Justice Bhagwati in S. P. Gupta (1982), the judgment that liberalised standing.

bank.q: With reference to the impact of PIL on the power of courts, consider the following:
s: It positioned the judiciary as a policy enforcer and guardian of governance ethics.
It produced green benches and vigilance commissions.
It produced guidelines in the absence of legislation, as in Vishaka.
bank.e: All three are correct — and together they explain both the achievement and the overreach critique.
